learningObjectives: Read the the ma, ya, ra and wa rows, plus ン in katakana.
Hand-write each new katakana shape with a steady stroke order.
Tell apart look-alike katakana by the direction and position of their small strokes.
Read familiar loanwords by joining one sound at a time.
Hear a word and choose the matching katakana spelling.

explanation.recap: The na and ha rows gave you the last big sound change: ハ can become バ or パ. These final rows complete the map and let you read familiar labels all around you.
explanation.intro: Katakana writes the same Japanese sound system you already know. Today the work is visual: learn the shapes in the ma, ya, ra and wa rows, plus ン, then let a familiar word give each shape a job. Read in short beats; one katakana normally carries one sound.

grammarPoints.pattern: カタカナ 一字 = 一つの 音
grammarPoints.meaning: one katakana sign usually holds one Japanese sound
grammarPoints.explanation: Katakana is not an English spelling system. Read each sign in order and give it one clean Japanese beat. Long words are not rushed: カ・メ・ラ is ka-me-ra. When a word has a long bar, stretch the vowel before it gently.
grammarPoints.watchFor: Do not guess from English spelling. Trust the katakana sounds on the page.
grammarPoints.commonError: Trying to give one sign two English sounds. Keep a single beat for each sign.

examples.note: Read the signs one by one.
The word is built from steady beats.

grammarPoints.nameJa: だくてん・半だくてん
grammarPoints.meaning: small marks can change a consonant sound
grammarPoints.explanation: Some katakana gain two small dakuten strokes, and the ハ row can gain a small handakuten circle. These marks are not decoration. They change the sound, so keep them small but visible.
grammarPoints.watchFor: The marks sit at the upper right of the character they change.
grammarPoints.commonError: Writing the mark in the middle of the character, where it becomes hard to read.

examples.note: Two small strokes voice the sound.

mission.title: The label finder
mission.prompt: Find four katakana labels around you: on food, a screen, a book, or an imagined shop shelf. Read them aloud and keep one that you want to remember.
successCriteria: You identify four katakana words or labels.
You read each one in separate Japanese sound beats.
You write one word with the small marks in the right place if it has them.
You say one meaning without relying on an English spelling guess.
